methodological_rigor.justification: The study is a long-term secondary analysis of SWOG S0016, a phase 3 randomized trial (n=531), with a median follow-up of 15.5 years and 50% of surviving patients having more than 15 years of follow-up, an exceptional retention record for FL cohorts. Statistical methods are appropriate and well-chosen: Kaplan-Meier for OS/PFS, Aalen-Johansen with Gray tests and Fine-Gray subdistribution hazards for competing-risk cumulative incidence, multivariable Cox for prognostic factors, and a log-normal parametric mixture cure model selected by AIC with CIs via flexsurvcure. Sensitivity analyses are a key strength: varying maximum follow-up times, simulating missed events (cure estimate robust at 34% even assuming 50% missed progressions post-10 years), and an alternate spline-based nonmixture model. Limitations include lack of central imaging/pathology review at relapse, no formal multiplicity adjustment for multiple subgroup cure estimates, and inherent model-dependence of mixture cure models under heavy censoring, all of which are at least partially acknowledged.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: This is a secondary long-term analysis of an individual multicenter randomized phase 3 trial (SWOG S0016, NCT00006721), supporting a 1b Oxford classification. Clinical relevance is very high: the findings directly challenge the long-held doctrine that advanced-stage FL is incurable with standard chemoimmunotherapy, with a 42% model-based cure rate and plateauing cumulative incidence curves and a declining relapse rate from 6.8% to 0.6% between the first 5 years and years 15-20. The paper provides concrete implications for patient counseling at diagnosis, modification of long-term surveillance intensity (transition to primary care after 10 years), and benchmarking for first-line trial design against emerging novel agents. Endpoints are patient-relevant (OS, PFS, cause-specific mortality, second cancers).

reporting_quality.justification: CONSORT is the applicable standard as this is a long-term follow-up and secondary analysis of a phase 3 RCT, and the manuscript explicitly states adherence to CONSORT. Reporting is thorough: trial registration (NCT00006721), IRB approval and informed consent are described, eligibility, intervention, randomization, patient flow (eFigure 1), pre-specified primary endpoints (PFS/OS), prognostic factor analyses, adverse events including second malignancies and AML/MDS, and detailed subgroup and sensitivity analyses are reported. Minor gaps include no explicit statement of blinding (though not applicable to this long-term update), no formal risk-of-bias assessment, and pre-specification status of the cure modeling vs. the original protocol is not fully clarified. Data/code availability is weak in the blinded text: analyses rely on the public flexsurvcure R package but there is no mention of a public repository, access policy, or deposited code; individual patient data from SWOG trials typically require application through NCTN but this is not described in what remains.

novelty_literature.justification: The novelty is empirical and conceptual: this is, to the reviewers' reading, the longest prospective modern-era follow-up of a frontline FL RCT with formal relative-survival cure modeling, demonstrating a plateau in cumulative incidence and estimating a 42% cure fraction after a single course of CHOP-based chemoimmunotherapy without maintenance. This directly challenges the entrenched view that advanced FL is incurable, which few prior studies have attempted with this statistical framework (prior 10-year S0016 report, Watanabe JCOG0203 at 15y without cure model, StiL NHL1, FOLL05, PRIMA, GALLIUM all cited as having shorter follow-up or no cure modeling). The underlying trial and treatment comparison are not new (initial and 10-year results previously published), so the novelty is the extended follow-up plus cure-model application rather than a new intervention or mechanism, keeping this at a 4 rather than 5.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is clearly written, logically organized, and uses the JAMA-style structured abstract (question, findings, meaning) that accurately summarizes the quantitative results. Methods are concise but complete, results map cleanly to the figures and tables and give both PFS/OS point estimates with CIs and granular temporal relapse rates, and the discussion contextualizes findings against FOLL05, PRIMA, GALLIUM, StiL NHL1, JCOG0203, and RELEVANCE without over-claiming beyond the data. Figure and table captions are informative and standalone-interpretable; the strengths/limitations section is honest about residual uncertainty (loss to follow-up, no central relapse review, declining use of RIT). Minor issues: a few typographical errors (e.g., '31 CI%' in a FLIPI 3-5 cure estimate, '95 CI%' for an sHR), and some repetition between results and discussion of the plateau argument.

key_strengths: Exceptional 15.5-year median follow-up of a phase 3 RCT (SWOG S0016) with 50% of survivors having more than 15 years of follow-up, among the longest in modern-era frontline FL
Rigorous statistical framework combining Kaplan-Meier, Aalen-Johansen/Fine-Gray competing-risk analysis, and a parametric mixture relative-survival cure model with AIC-based model selection
Robust sensitivity analyses demonstrating the ~42% cure estimate holds even under assumptions of 50% missed progressions beyond 10 years, and under an alternate spline-based nonmixture cure model
Paradigm-challenging clinical message with concrete implications for patient counseling, long-term surveillance strategy, and benchmarking of novel first-line regimens
Transparent, balanced reporting of second cancers and cause-specific mortality including an elevated AML/MDS signal in the CHOP-RIT arm (sHR 3.8, 95% CI 1.1-13.5)
key_concerns: Cure modeling appears largely post-hoc relative to the original SWOG S0016 protocol, and pre-specification status for the 15-year cure analysis is not explicitly stated
No central pathology or imaging review at relapse limits ability to distinguish FL recurrence from histologic transformation, acknowledged but not quantified

Loss to follow-up and non-mandatory imaging after 7 years create residual uncertainty despite sensitivity analyses; model-dependence of mixture cure estimates under heavy right-censoring remains a soft underbelly of the primary claim
Limited generalizability: predominantly non-Hispanic White population and half the cohort received radioimmunotherapy that is now rarely used in practice
Data and code sharing posture is weak in the blinded text; beyond citing the public flexsurvcure R package, there is no mention of code deposition or an individual patient data access pathway
Minor typographical errors in reported confidence intervals (e.g., '31 CI%', '95 CI%') should be corrected
chief_reviewer.rationale: A methodologically solid, statistically rigorous long-term RCT follow-up with a potentially paradigm-shifting message for FL that is well-supported by competing-risk and cure-model analyses with multiple sensitivity checks; the content profile (large national RCT, practice-informing conclusion, strong statistics) is consistent with top-tier oncology journals, warranting Tier 1 with minor revisions to clarify pre-specification, central review limitations, and data/code availability.
